title: Pulled Pork BBQ
subtitle: slow-roasted pork shoulder with smoky rub
excerpt: Pork shoulder rubbed with smoked spices and roasted low and slow until it falls apart. A tangy vinegar sauce goes over at the end. Pile it into rolls with coleslaw for a summer crowd-pleaser.
sourceNotes: Pulled pork is one of the four main styles of American BBQ. The slow-smoke tradition comes from the Carolinas and the Southern states, where pit masters have perfected it over generations.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze the pulled pork in portions with some of the cooking juices.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Apply the rub the night before and refrigerate. The spices will penetrate the meat further.

content.text: The key to pulled pork is low, slow heat and patience. Do not rush by turning up the oven. The fat and connective tissue need several hours to break down fully. Score the pork shoulder all over to help the rub penetrate.
Preheat the oven to 150C (fan 130C / gas 2). Score the pork shoulder all over with deep cuts about 2cm apart.
Mix the smoked paprika, brown sugar, cumin, cayenne, garlic, worcestershire sauce, and honey into a thick paste.
Rub the paste all over the pork, pressing it into the scored cuts.
Pour the stock into the roasting tin. Place the pork on top. Cover tightly with foil.
Roast for 5 to 6 hours, basting every hour. Remove the foil for the last 30 minutes to crisp the outside.
The pork is ready when you can pull it apart easily with two forks.
Rest for 30 minutes, then shred the meat. Drizzle over the cooking juices and the apple cider vinegar.
Pile into rolls with coleslaw and extra sauce on the side.

items.fix: Return to the oven covered and cook for another 30 to 60 minutes. The collagen needs more time to break down.

items.symptom: Outside burned but inside not done
items.cause: Foil removed too early or oven too hot
items.fix: Keep the foil on until the last 30 minutes. Pork shoulder can handle long cooking at low temperatures.

items.cause: Rub not applied into the cuts
items.fix: Score deeply next time and work the rub into every cut. Applying the rub the night before makes a big difference.

content.text: Pulled pork BBQ is a Southern American tradition with roots in the Carolinas. Pit masters there have been slow-smoking pork shoulders over hardwood coals for hundreds of years. The style spread across the South and eventually the whole country. Today you will find pulled pork at everything from roadside shacks to high-street restaurants.
